fact: The Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) program, which includes a peg transfer task, is required for general surgery residents in the US to be eligible for board certification.
source: SAGES / American College of Surgeons, Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery; ABS requirement since 2009

fact: In a randomized, double-blind trial, residents trained on a virtual reality laparoscopic simulator made about six times fewer errors in a real gallbladder removal than untrained peers, and worked 29% faster.
source: Seymour NE et al., Annals of Surgery, 2002

fact: The fulcrum effect: because instruments pivot at the port in the body wall, moving your hand left moves the instrument tip right. Trainees must unlearn natural hand-eye mapping.
source: Gallagher AG et al., Surgical Endoscopy, 1998

fact: Laparoscopy shows a 3D body on a 2D monitor, so surgeons lose stereoscopic depth perception and must rely on shadows, texture and instrument cues.
source: Standard minimally invasive surgery training literature; e.g. SAGES FLS Manual, 2014

fact: Laparoscopic bile duct injury is a rare but serious complication, and a study of 252 such cases found that most were caused by perceptual errors (misreading the anatomy) rather than a lack of knowledge or technical skill.
source: Way LW et al., Annals of Surgery, 2003

fact: OSATS, the Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills, scores a trainee's operative technique on items such as respect for tissue, time and motion, and flow of operation. It showed good reliability and validity against expert ratings.
source: Martin JA et al., British Journal of Surgery, 1997

fact: Everyone has a small physiological hand tremor, usually around 8 to 12 Hz, that can be made worse by fatigue, caffeine or stress. Surgeons manage it with technique such as braced wrists, supported elbows and slow, deliberate movement.
source: Elble RJ, Koller WC, Tremor, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1990

fact: Surgical skill is measurable and matters: in a study of bariatric surgeons rated from operative video by peers, lower technical skill ratings were linked to higher complication rates for their patients.
source: Birkmeyer JD et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2013

fact: Practising on simulators lets trainees make mistakes without harming patients. A large meta-analysis found that simulation-based training improves knowledge, skills and behaviours far more than no training.

Adverse events affect a notable share of hospital patients, and a systematic review found that around half of them were judged potentially preventable. This is why deliberate practice and objective assessment matter.
source: de Vries EN et al., Quality and Safety in Health Care, 2008

fact: Proficiency-based training, where trainees practice until they hit an expert benchmark rather than for a fixed time, is the model behind the FLS and Seymour VR studies.
source: Gallagher AG et al., Annals of Surgery, 2005 (virtual reality training: proficiency-based approach)

fact: Simple low-cost box trainers (a box, a camera and basic tools) can build laparoscopic skills that transfer to the operating room, which matters in hospitals without expensive simulation labs.
source: Orzech N et al., Surgical Endoscopy, 2012 (systematic review of box trainers vs. VR trainers)
